Name: David Seidman
Question: What degree will help my progress from a senior software engineer to a software engineering manager?
Answer: None. I have never promoted someone to manager or hired them as a manager because of a degree. Management is about people skills and leadership, and you don't learn those in a classroom. Learn and demonstrate those skills in your job, and you'll become qualified to be a manager. To be fair, you could get an MBA and go work for the kind of company that hires MBAs as technical managers. But you'll find yourself working for someone who was also hired because of their MBA, and that person may not have any clue about software engineering. You're likely to be given impossible assignments on impossible timelines and have your performance evaluated by someone who knows nothing about your field. It's not likely to be a good experience. And you'll have paid $200k and given up two years of experience for the privilege. Just step up and be a leader in your current job, and you'll find management opportunities open up for you.

Name: David Seidman
Question: In the recruiting process, do engineering managers at Google also have to solve algorithm and data structure tasks?
Answer: I was asked to solve one fairly simple coding problem. It took half of one interview. I also spent 1.5 interviews answering security technical questions. I'm a Security Engineering Manager, not a Software Engineering Manager. I suspect that SWE Managers write code in place of the security technical questions.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What is your perspective of the desire to work at Facebook given the continued backlash?
Answer: Based on what friends are telling me, there does seem to have been a decrease in interest in working for Facebook. There is a perception that Zuckerberg has intentionally allowed political misinformation to avoid angering the Trump administration. In addition to being directly distasteful to many potential employees, it also gives the impression that Zuckerberg is amoral or unethical - not endearing qualities in a potential boss. It's also becoming increasingly clear that Facebook has not made much progress in addressing the issues of propaganda and partisan toxicity that plagued it in the 2016 election, nor has it fully recovered trust after the Cambridge Analytica scandal. Not many people these days view Facebook as a force for good. Facebook is still able to attract many strong employees. They pay well and have good benefits, they have a good corporate culture, and they have an extremely important product with a billion users and interesting technical challenges. But their star has lost a little bit of its shine.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Do good employees make good managers?
Answer: Being hardworking, smart and a good communicator and leader help a person succeed as an employee and as a manager. Being very technically skilled is important for being a good employee but not required to be a good manager. And management is its own kind of technical skill that must be learned. Usually if someone has those positive traits required for management, they can learn how to do it well. The error many organizations make is to promote a strong technical contributor because that person wants to be a manager, even if the person doesn't have the right soft skills or attitude to do well at it. It never works out well.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What are the basics of starting a big company like Google or Apple?
Answer: You need a few factors to try to become a billion dollar tech company. You need a large total addressable market, ideally something close to “everyone”. For massive profits you need massive scale. You need a defensible competitive position with barriers to entry. You can't make a billion dollars if other companies can copy your idea. A common barrier to entry is a “network effect”, where a product with more users is inherently a better product, so that once one company has a large user base it becomes impossible to challenge. You need a strong team that can build the right technology, manage finances without running out of money, and sell the product to customers. It's common for a startup to be funded mostly based on the past success of its founders. You need to get lucky. You need the right idea with the right execution at the right time, and even then an unexpected event outside your control could still destroy your company. I knew someone whose big product launch happened on September 11, 2001. The business did not succeed. Lastly, you need the desire to keep running your business even after you could sell it for millions. Almost every billion dollar company rejected buyout offers that would have made its founders multimillionaires. It's not very rational from a financial perspective - there's not much you can buy with a billion dollars that you can't buy with $50 million - but something made those founders hang on and stay independent. It might be a belief in the vision of the product, in the future of the company or in the founders themselves. But for whatever reason, those founders held on until the company became truly giant.
